newsitem.title: ITALY: U.N. official dismisses China food shortage fear.
newsitem.headline: U.N. official dismisses China food shortage fear.

text.p: The head of the U.N.'s food agency lavished praise on China's agricultural "miracle" on Tuesday and dismissed fears the country would soon be unable to feed itself.

Jacques Diouf, director general of the Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), told Chinese television that heavy rural spending highlighted Beijing's determination to keep its 1.2 billion people fed despite relatively scarce land for its farms.

"Naturally the situation of China is, even today, already a miracle because China has 22 percent of the world population but only seven percent of the world's arable land," Diouf said in an interview with CCTV Chinese television.

He was speaking on the eve of a five-day U.N-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome, where one leading food expert warned on Tuesday that China would find it increasingly difficult to grow the grain it needs to sustain its booming economy.

Lester Brown, president of the Worldwatch Institute, a private Washington-ba sed monitor of food supplies, told a news conference that China was losing croplands at a record rate, turning it from a net grain exporter two years ago to the second biggest importer behind Japan in 1995.

Asked about Brown's forecasts that China would be unable to keep up with its domestic needs, Diouf said Beijing was already working hard to increase its food security by investing some $80 billion in flood and water control.
"This is an indication of the will and capacity of the government to invest in this sector and satisfy its needs," Diouf said.

Chinese Premier Li Peng is expected to address the five-day summit, intended to find ways to eradicate hunger of producing enough food to nourish an extra three billion people expected to be born worldwide over the next 30 years.

Brown, who has written a book on China's food needs, said it would continue to step up grain imports in the next decade to satisfy the demands of a wealthier population. People with extra money in their pockets tend to eat more meat, requiring grain for animal feed, he said.
FAO's own researchers argue with this, saying China has plenty of scope to increase its domestic grain yields and make up for the loss of arable land to factories.
China is the world's largest producer of wheat but imported some 11 million tonnes last year to supplement its harvest.
This year it predicts a record crop and most Western analysts expect its imports to drop by around half.
China's imports have politically sensitive implications for several other nations at the summit, some of whom say their own food import bills have risen because of the impact on prices.
Wheat prices hit a record in April this year because global demand rose at a time when stocks were at a 20-year low.
Brown told Reuters he felt that least developed nations in Africa would be the "big losers" from China's rising dependence on world markets over the next 10 years.
But Diouf said China had been generous in giving help to developing nations in the southern hemisphere, citing projects to help Mali and Ethiopia increase food production.
